script.opening: "I had a blood test for a pre-op check and the doctor mentioned my lymphocytes were high and used the word ‘leukaemia’. I’ve been beside myself — my wife’s in pieces. But the strange thing is I feel completely fine. Does this mean I’m dying?"

facts.text: Pre-op assessment for a hernia repair 2 weeks ago. "Just that one type of white cell was high and it might be leukaemia. Then I stopped listening." Has the clinic letter (if asked what it says: lymphocytes 11.2, everything else normal; the pre-op doctor "felt my neck and tummy and said nothing was enlarged").

No night sweats, no fevers, no weight loss, not tired. No lumps in the neck, armpits or groin that he can feel (will feel his neck on camera if asked). No more infections than usual. No bruising or bleeding.
"Fit as a fiddle." Walks the dog 5 miles a day. Inguinal hernia, otherwise well. No medicines. No allergies. Had his flu jab last year; doesn’t know about pneumococcal or shingles vaccines.
Retired teacher. Married to Jean for 42 years — she is "in pieces". Two grown-up children. Non-smoker, 10 units a week. Gardener — out in the sun a lot.
"Chemotherapy, hospital, dying quickly." His brother died of acute leukaemia at 50 — only if the doctor explores why he is so frightened.
Polite, controlled, frightened underneath. Ask "Then why is it called leukaemia?" and "So no chemotherapy?". Relief if the doctor explains calmly. Would like Jean to come to the next appointment.

ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — his brother’s death from acute leukaemia, and leaving his wife. Also wonders if the hernia operation will go ahead.

cues: "Does this mean I’m dying?" — honest, calibrated explanation needed.
"My wife’s in pieces" — offer to involve her.
"My brother died of leukaemia" (if fear is explored) — why the word is so frightening.

Assesses for features/staging pointers (lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, B symptoms, anaemia/thrombocytopenia, infections)
Refers to HAEMATOLOGY for confirmation, staging and management through the local pathway (faster if cytopenias, bulky nodes, B symptoms or a rapidly rising count), and informs the pre-operative team
Explains "WATCH AND WAIT" — many early-stage patients need no treatment for years with near-normal life expectancy; treatment reserved for progressive/symptomatic disease

Counsels INFECTION risk (influenza, pneumococcal, COVID-19 vaccines, Shingrix eligibility, avoid live vaccines, prompt treatment, reporting fevers/recurrent infections), skin-cancer risk, and what to monitor/report
Handles the word "leukaemia" with HONEST, calibrated reassurance — acknowledging it is a cancer but often very indolent — without false promises or minimising, supporting the patient and his wife
Paces the information and invites questions, agreeing the monitoring and watch-and-wait plan together so he understands why no treatment now is the right, active choice

Safety-nets and follows up: haematology referral, what to report (B symptoms, infections, new lumps, bleeding), vaccination, and review — honest communication + indolent-CLL recognition + watch-and-wait explanation

worked.txt: "I can see how frightening that word is — take a breath, and let me explain properly, because the reality is often far more reassuring than it sounds."

"Your blood shows a raised number of one type of white cell, which does look like a condition called CLL — chronic lymphocytic leukaemia. It is technically a blood cancer, but I want to be honest AND reassuring: it’s very often slow-growing, and many people — especially diagnosed by chance while feeling well, like you — never need treatment and live a normal lifespan."

"Let me check a few things — any lumps, night sweats, weight loss, frequent infections? … None. And I’ll feel for glands and your spleen. I’ll refer you to the blood specialists to confirm it and see what stage it is, and let the team doing your pre-op check know."

"For many people at an early stage, the approach is ‘watch and wait’ — simply monitoring with blood tests, no treatment unless it ever becomes active. That’s not neglect; it’s because treating early doesn’t help and the condition often stays quiet for years."

"One practical thing: CLL can lower your defences, so keep up with vaccinations — flu, pneumonia, COVID — and we’ll check whether you should have the shingles vaccine. Avoid live vaccines, and see us promptly with infections or fevers. Use sun cream too, as skin cancers are a bit more common with CLL."

"Bring your wife next time if it helps — I’ll explain it to you both. Report any new lumps, drenching sweats, weight loss, unusual bruising or repeated infections. I’ll get the referral moving and we’ll go through everything together."

f.learning: A persistent, isolated mature LYMPHOCYTOSIS in an older adult is commonly CHRONIC LYMPHOCYTIC LEUKAEMIA (CLL), confirmed by blood film and FLOW CYTOMETRY/immunophenotyping (iwCLL 2018, international: at least 5 × 10⁹/L clonal B lymphocytes; lower counts without node or organ involvement are monoclonal B-cell lymphocytosis), and is often INDOLENT and frequently diagnosed INCIDENTALLY in well, asymptomatic patients. Assess for clinical features and staging pointers — lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, B symptoms (unexplained weight loss, drenching night sweats, fevers), anaemia/thrombocytopenia, and recurrent infections — and refer to HAEMATOLOGY for confirmation, staging (Binet/Rai) and a management plan. The reassuring reality to explain is "WATCH AND WAIT": many early-stage CLL patients need no treatment for years (sometimes never), are monitored with periodic bloods/review, and can have a near-normal life expectancy, with treatment reserved for progressive/symptomatic disease (rising counts/organomegaly, cytopenias, B symptoms). Counsel infection risk — CLL impairs immunity, so vaccinations (influenza, pneumococcal, COVID-19; check Shingrix eligibility; avoid live vaccines — Green Book), sun protection because skin cancers are more common, prompt treatment of infections, and reporting fevers/recurrent infections matter — and advise what to monitor/report (B symptoms, new lumps, infections, bleeding/bruising, fatigue). The communication core is the word "leukaemia": be honest that it is a cancer but provide calibrated reassurance (often very indolent, many never need treatment, near-normal life expectancy in many) without false promises or minimising, supporting both patient and family. Referral for a well patient with isolated lymphocytosis and normal haemoglobin and platelets is usually through the local haematology pathway, with faster review for cytopenias, bulky nodes, B symptoms or a rapid rise (BSH 2022); NICE NG12 very urgent FBC applies to adults with features of leukaemia, and a suspected cancer pathway referral is not the route once flow cytometry suggests CLL in a well patient. Inform the pre-operative team.

knowledge.guideline: [1] iwCLL guidelines for diagnosis and treatment of CLL (Hallek et al., Blood 2018) (international) · NICE NG12 Suspected cancer: recognition and referral (2015, last updated 15 April 2026) · [2] British Society for Haematology guideline for the treatment of chronic lymphocytic leukaemia (2025) · [4] UKHSA Green Book chapters 6, 7, 19, 25 and 28a · [5] NICE NG47 (haematological cancers: improving outcomes, 2016)
knowledge.summary: An isolated, persistent lymphocytosis of mature B cells in an older adult is most often chronic lymphocytic leukaemia. CLL is diagnosed with a clonal B-lymphocyte count of at least 5 × 10⁹/L confirmed by flow cytometry. Most people found incidentally have early-stage disease that is monitored without treatment, and many never need treatment. Refer to haematology for confirmation and staging, check for symptoms, lymph nodes, spleen and liver enlargement and cytopenias, and give infection and vaccination advice. Be honest that it is a blood cancer, and just as clear that for many it behaves like a long-term condition.

points.t: iwCLL [1] defines CLL as at least 5 × 10⁹/L clonal B lymphocytes in the blood, sustained, with a characteristic immunophenotype on flow cytometry. Below that level, without lymph node or organ involvement, the finding is monoclonal B-cell lymphocytosis (MBL), which progresses slowly in a minority.

Ask about night sweats, fevers, weight loss, fatigue and recurrent infections, and check for lymph nodes, spleen and liver (by the patient’s report and the recorded examination, or arrange an in-person examination). Check the full count for anaemia and low platelets. These findings guide urgency and staging (Binet or Rai), which haematology confirms [1][2].

NICE NG12 [3] recommends a very urgent FBC to assess for leukaemia in adults with features such as pallor, persistent fatigue, unexplained fever, persistent or recurrent infection, generalised lymphadenopathy, unexplained bruising or bleeding, and hepatosplenomegaly. A well patient with an isolated lymphocytosis and normal haemoglobin and platelets can usually be referred through the local haematology pathway; cytopenias, bulky nodes, B symptoms or a rapidly rising count need faster review.

Early-stage, asymptomatic CLL is monitored, not treated, because early treatment has not been shown to improve survival [1][2]. Treatment starts when the disease is active: progressive marrow failure, bulky or symptomatic nodes or spleen, a rapidly rising count, or significant symptoms. Many people never need treatment.

CLL reduces immunity even when untreated. Offer annual influenza vaccine, pneumococcal vaccine and COVID-19 vaccine as per the current seasonal programme, and check eligibility for non-live shingles vaccine (Shingrix) under the Green Book [4]. Live vaccines should be avoided in significant immunosuppression [4]. Advise prompt review of fevers and infections.

Skin cancers are more common in CLL, so advise sun protection and reporting new skin lesions. Autoimmune haemolysis or low platelets can occur. Haematology care is delivered through a specialist multidisciplinary team (NICE NG47 [5]).

model.text: Hello Mr Ross, I’m Dr Morgan. How can I help today?

I had a blood test for a pre-op check and the doctor mentioned my lymphocytes were high and used the word ‘leukaemia’. I’ve been beside myself. My wife’s in pieces. But the strange thing is I feel completely fine. Does this mean I’m dying?

I can see how frightening that word has been for you both. I want to answer your question honestly, and I think what I say will be more reassuring than you expect. Can I ask a few questions and go through the examination from your pre-op clinic first, so I can give you an accurate picture?
model.why: Acknowledges fear and signals calibrated reassurance

model.text: Please.
What exactly were you told about the result?
Just that one type of white cell was high and it might be leukaemia. Then I stopped listening.
That’s very understandable. Have you had drenching sweats at night, fevers, or lost weight without trying?
No, nothing like that.
Any lumps in your neck, armpits or groin, or a feeling of fullness under your left ribs?
Not that I’ve noticed.
Have you been getting more infections than usual, or any unusual bruising or bleeding?
No. I’m fit as a fiddle.
When you heard ‘leukaemia’, what did you picture?
Chemotherapy, hospital, dying quickly.
And what worries you most?
Leaving my wife. She’s terrified.
At the pre-op clinic two weeks ago they checked for lymph glands in your neck, armpits and groin and felt your tummy for the spleen and liver — none were enlarged.
Go ahead.

Your blood test shows a raised number of lymphocytes, and the other parts of your blood count, the red cells and platelets, weren’t reported as low. The pattern looks like a condition called chronic lymphocytic leukaemia, or CLL. I won’t pretend it isn’t a type of blood cancer. But it’s very different from the leukaemia people picture.
Different how?

In most people found by chance like you, it’s very slow. Many people live with it for many years without it causing trouble, and many never need any treatment at all. So no, this does not mean you’re dying.
model.why: Calibrated reassurance answering his direct question

model.text: Really? Then why is it called leukaemia?
Because it comes from the blood cells. The name is the same family, but the behaviour is completely different.

I’ll refer you to the blood specialists to confirm it and work out the stage. For most people at your stage, the plan is ‘watch and wait’: regular blood tests and check-ups, and treatment only if it ever becomes active. That’s not doing nothing. Treating early doesn’t help, so we keep you well and keep watching.
So no chemotherapy?

Not now, and possibly never. If treatment is ever needed, the modern options are often tablets. One practical thing: CLL can lower your defences against infection. So keep up your flu, pneumonia and COVID vaccines, and we’ll check whether you should have the shingles vaccine. Avoid live vaccines, and see us promptly if you get a fever or an infection.
I can do that.
I’ll also let the team doing your pre-op check know about the referral, so they can plan with the haematologists. Would it help if your wife came with you next time, so I can explain it to her too?
model.why: Coordinates care; involves his wife with consent

model.text: Yes, she’d like that.

Before you see the specialist, come back sooner if you notice new lumps, drenching night sweats, weight loss, fevers, repeated infections, or unusual bruising or bleeding. And use sun cream, as skin cancers are a bit more common with CLL. What will you tell your wife tonight?
That it’s a slow type that often never needs treatment, I’m being referred, I need my vaccines, and we’ll come back together.
That’s a very good summary.

pitfalls.intro: The clinical content is modest. This station is about telling a frightened man the truth in a way he can live with.

items.why: An unanswered question keeps the fear alive.
It is a cancer; he will learn that from the haematologist.
items.fix: Be honest and put it in context.

items.fail: No symptom screen or check of the examination.
items.why: B symptoms, nodes, spleen and cytopenias change urgency.
Flow cytometry confirmation and staging are specialist tasks.
items.fix: Refer through the local pathway, faster if features are present.
Vaccines as per the Green Book; no live vaccines; prompt review of infections.

items.fail: Presenting watch and wait as doing nothing.
items.fix: Explain why monitoring is the right, active choice.

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: The clinical content is modest. This station is about telling a frightened man the truth in a way he can live with.

items.why: An unanswered question keeps the fear alive.
It is a cancer; he will learn that from the haematologist.
items.fix: Be honest and put it in context.

items.fail: No symptom screen or check of the examination.
items.why: B symptoms, nodes, spleen and cytopenias change urgency.
Flow cytometry confirmation and staging are specialist tasks.
items.fix: Refer through the local pathway, faster if features are present.
Vaccines as per the Green Book; no live vaccines; prompt review of infections.

items.fail: Presenting watch and wait as doing nothing.
items.fix: Explain why monitoring is the right, active choice.
